guide.summary: Unit 8 covers modes and other scales, and the formal structures of common-practice and popular music, from binary and ternary forms to sonata form and the twelve-bar blues.

sections.heading: Modes and other scales
sections.body: The church modes can be heard on the white keys: Ionian (C, major), Dorian (D: natural minor with raised 6), Phrygian (E: natural minor with lowered 2), Lydian (F: major with raised 4), Mixolydian (G: major with lowered 7), Aeolian (A, natural minor), and Locrian (B, diminished tonic triad, rarely used). Other scales include the major pentatonic (1 2 3 5 6), minor pentatonic, the whole-tone scale (six notes, all whole steps, no perfect fifths), the chromatic scale, and the blues scale. To identify a mode, compare it with the major or natural minor scale on the same tonic.

sections.heading: Small forms
sections.body: Binary form (AB, each section usually repeated) often has a first section ending away from tonic (e.g., in the dominant). Rounded binary returns part of A at the end of the second section (A B A'). Ternary form (ABA) has a contrasting, self-contained middle section and a full return. Strophic songs repeat the same music for each verse; through-composed songs set each verse to new music. Theme and variations alters a theme in melody, rhythm, harmony, or texture.

sections.heading: Larger and popular forms
sections.body: Rondo alternates a recurring refrain with contrasting episodes (ABACA or ABACABA). Sonata form has an exposition (first theme in tonic, transition, second theme in the dominant or relative major, closing), a development that fragments and modulates, and a recapitulation that returns themes in the tonic, sometimes with a coda. The twelve-bar blues follows I I I I | IV IV I I | V IV I I (with variants), and popular songs use verse–chorus structures.

sections.heading: Worked example: identifying a mode
sections.body: To identify a mode, compare the scale with major or natural minor on the same tonic. D–E–F–G–A–B–C–D compared with D natural minor (D–E–F–G–A–B♭–C–D) has a raised sixth (B♮), so it is Dorian. G–A–B–C–D–E–F–G compared with G major has a lowered seventh (F♮), so it is Mixolydian. F–G–A–B–C–D–E–F compared with F major has a raised fourth (B♮), so it is Lydian. E–F–G–A–B–C–D–E compared with E natural minor has a lowered second (F♮), so it is Phrygian.

sections.heading: Listening for form
sections.body: Track returning material and key changes. In binary form, listen for a contrasting second section that may begin away from tonic. In rounded binary, the opening returns partway through the second section. In ternary, a contrasting middle section is followed by a complete return. In rondo, a refrain returns between episodes. In sonata form, listen for two contrasting themes in different keys in the exposition, a development that fragments and modulates, and a recapitulation in the tonic.

sections.heading: Sight-singing strategies
sections.body: Before singing, identify the key, find the tonic, and scan for leaps and accidentals. Sing the scale and tonic triad to orient yourself, then choose a comfortable tempo and keep a steady beat. If you make a mistake, keep going rather than restarting; rhythm and pitch accuracy across the whole melody earn credit.

sections.heading: Common errors
sections.body: Students confuse Dorian with Aeolian and miss partial returns in rounded binary.

sections.heading: Worked example: analyzing a song form
sections.body: A popular song might have the structure verse–chorus–verse–chorus–bridge–chorus. The verses share music but have different lyrics, the chorus repeats both music and lyrics, and the bridge provides contrast before the final chorus. Classical analogies include strophic form for verses and ternary-like contrast for the bridge. Twelve-bar blues uses a fixed harmonic pattern: I for four bars, IV for two, I for two, V and IV for one bar each, and I for the final two.

sections.heading: Key terms
sections.body: Know the church modes, pentatonic, whole-tone, and chromatic scales, binary, rounded binary, ternary, strophic, through-composed, theme and variations, rondo, sonata form, and twelve-bar blues.

sections.heading: Practice routine
sections.body: Practice sight-singing a short melody every day, and listen to examples of each form.

sections.heading: Free-response connection
sections.body: Aural multiple-choice questions often ask about form and mode, so listen to many examples.

sections.heading: Final tip
sections.body: Compare every mode to major or natural minor on the same tonic.

keyTakeaways: Binary vs rounded binary vs ternary.
commonMistakes: Calling rounded binary 'ternary' when the return is partial and within section 2.
Placing the second theme of the recapitulation in the dominant.
examTips: Compare modes to major/minor on the same tonic.

Track key areas in sonata form.

practice.sampleResponse:
a. D E F G A B C D is D Dorian (natural minor with a raised sixth, B♮).
b. G A B C D E F G is G Mixolydian (major with a lowered seventh, F♮).
c. E F G A B C D E is E Phrygian, identified by the half step from E to F (lowered second).
d. A form of ||: A :||: B A' :|| is rounded binary.
e. A refrain alternating with contrasting episodes (ABACA) is a rondo.
f. The development section fragments themes and moves through several keys.
